sentences: Seen from above, a child in white runs across the ochre ground of a park.
A red ball rolls ahead, and a dark shadow falls in front of the child.
The rest of the picture is filled with the deep shade of trees.
This is The Ball, painted in 1899 by the Swiss-born artist Félix Vallotton.
It is oil on cardboard, later mounted on a wooden panel.
The picture is small, only about 49 by 62 centimetres, and it belongs to the Musée d'Orsay in Paris.
Vallotton was born in Lausanne, Switzerland, in 1865, and moved to Paris at sixteen to study art.
In the 1890s he was close to the Nabis, a group of young painters that included Pierre Bonnard and Édouard Vuillard.
His friends called him the foreign Nabi.
He first became known for his woodcuts, made of large areas of black and white with very little detail.
He also collected Japanese prints, and learned from them how to look down on a scene from above and how to use flat areas of colour.
Look closely at the child.
A wide yellow hat with a red ribbon sits on the head, and blond hair escapes from under the brim.
The white smock, buttoned at the back, flies out behind in the wind.
The little boots are a dull orange.
Now look at the red ball.
The child is running to chase it.
The ball, the child and the shadow are all simple, clear shapes, sitting sharply on the bright ground like cut paper.
Find the two figures standing far away.
They stand side by side, one in blue and one in white.
The museum describes them as two women.
Their pale colours echo the white of the running child.
But something is strange here.
The two women are tiny, so they must be far away.
Yet the picture is built from flat areas of colour, and it is hard to feel the distance.
The museum notes that the space seems flat and frontal.
Look at the light and the shade.
The sunny ochre ground and the dark mass of the trees face each other.
The edge of the shade spreads across the ground in scalloped curves.
The scene shows a happy game, yet the strong contrast gives it a feeling of quiet tension.
In the same year Vallotton married, and the following year he became a French citizen.
Parks and public gardens were favourite subjects of his friends Bonnard and Vuillard too.
The painting came to the French national collection in 1953, left by the collector Carle Dreyfus.
Step back and see the whole picture.
Between the open ground and the dark trees, one small child chasing one ball sets everything in motion.
Today, remember a moment from childhood when you ran after something with your whole heart.
